summary: Speaking from Bhagavad-gita 7.3, Indradyumna Swami explains that out of many thousands of men hardly one strives for perfection, and of those, hardly one truly knows Krishna. He traces how spiritual interest has declined across the four yugas (Satya, Treta, Dvapara, Kali) from nearly 100% down to about 25% today, and notes that Kali-yuga's darkness of ignorance began the moment Krishna's lotus feet left the earth about 5,000 years ago. The heart of the lecture is that the special gift of the human form of life is buddhi, intelligence (buddhi-yoga), which sets humans apart from the other 8,400,000 species and is meant to be used to inquire into the self, God, and one's eternal relationship with Him. He stresses that Bhagavad-gita is as valuable now as ever, since its purpose depends on whether one takes the goal of life to be material comfort or the awakening of divine consciousness, and he contrasts the two paths of pravritti-marga (material enjoyment) and nivritti-marga (renunciation leading to liberation and love of God). Using the story of Yudhishthira answering Yamaraja's questions, he underlines the most amazing thing in the world: everyone sees others die yet each person thinks he will live forever, so people foolishly invest everything in a temporary future while making no preparation for the certainty of death and the soul's transmigration to its next body. The merciful solution for this fallen age is the chanting of the Hare Krishna maha-mantra, glorified in scripture as the one good thing left in Kali-yuga, made available to everyone by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu who appeared 500 years ago. Indradyumna Swami concludes that this culture is not merely Indian but transcendental, that one must know God in detail in order to love Him, and that the strict pure lifestyle becomes possible only through the higher taste one gets by chanting the holy names.
key_points: Bhagavad-gita 7.3 (manushyanam sahasreshu): out of many thousands only a few seek perfection, and hardly one truly knows Krishna; the purport from Srila Prabhupada notes that even great impersonalists find it difficult to know Krishna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

The four yugas decline rather than improve, contrary to modern evolutionary theory: interest in liberation falls from about 99.999% in Satya-yuga to 75%, 50%, and roughly 25% in Kali-yuga, whose ignorance (compared to darkness after sunset) began when Krishna departed 5,000 years ago.

The unique gift of the human form is buddhi/intelligence (buddhi-yoga); just as God gives each of the 8,400,000 species a special ability (birds fly, fish swim, bears hibernate, butterflies are beautiful), humans receive intelligence, meant to see beyond maya and be used for self-realization (Vedanta-sutra as the Vedas in 'code,' like Morse code; athato brahma-jijnasa).

The Manipal University story: a student challenged the value of a 5,000-year-old book, and the Swami replied that its worth depends on whether one's goal of life is material enjoyment or awakening divine consciousness, citing Gandhi who always carried the Bhagavad-gita, and distinguishing pravritti-marga from nivritti-marga.

The Mahabharata story of Yudhishthira and Yamaraja (Dharmaraja) teaches the most amazing thing in the world: everyone witnesses others dying yet thinks he himself will live forever; likewise the soul transmigrates (BG 2.13; cells renew every seven years) and one's consciousness at death (BG 8.6) determines the next body, so one must prepare like packing before the bulldozers arrive.

Srila Prabhupada's story of the sculptor who made nine lifelike dioramas of himself to cheat death, but Yamaraja provoked his artistic ego by criticizing the work, exposing the real man and taking him away, illustrating that death cannot be tricked by material means (as Ravana's staircase to heaven failed).

The prescribed process for Kali-yuga is chanting the holy names: harer nama harer nama harer namaiva kevalam (Brihan-naradiya Purana) and kirtanad eva krishnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet (spoken by Sukadeva to Maharaja Parikshit), open to everyone; Chaitanya Mahaprabhu's movement (krishna-varnam tvishakrishnam) is transcendental, not merely Indian, and the pure regulative lifestyle (no meat, fish, eggs, onion, garlic, intoxication, illicit sex, or gambling) is sustained only by the higher taste of the Hare Krishna maha-mantra (Chanakya's principle of giving up something lower for something better).
references: Om namo bhagavate vasudevaya — the opening invocation (mangalacharana) chanted before the lecture.

Bhagavad-gita 7.3 — 'manushyanam sahasreshu kashchid yatati siddhaye, yatatam api siddhanam kashchin mam vetti tattvatah.' The central verse of the talk, read with Srila Prabhupada's purport: out of many thousands hardly one strives for perfection, and of those hardly one truly knows Krishna.
Brahma-samhita 5.1 — 'ishvarah paramah krishnah sac-cid-ananda-vigrahah, anadir adir govindah sarva-karana-karanam.' Quoted (twice) to establish Krishna as the Supreme Person and cause of all causes.

Bhagavad-gita 4.8 — 'paritranaya sadhunam vinashaya cha dushkritam...' Cited for Krishna's appearance to deliver His devotees, annihilate demons (Kamsa, Shishupala, Dantavakra, Jarasandha), and re-establish dharma.
Vedanta-sutra 1.1.1 — 'athato brahma-jijnasa.' Cited as the first aphorism / the forefathers' instruction that the human form is the time for inquiry into the self and the Absolute.

Bhagavad-gita 5.18 — 'vidya-vinaya-sampanne brahmane gavi hastini, shuni chaiva shvapake cha panditah sama-darshinah.' Cited for the sage's equal vision toward a learned brahmana, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and a dog-eater.

Bhagavad-gita 8.16 — 'abrahma-bhuvanal lokah punar avartino 'rjuna, mam upetya tu kaunteya punar janma na vidyate.' Cited that from the highest planet to the lowest all are places of misery with repeated birth and death, but one who reaches Krishna's abode is never reborn.

Bhagavad-gita 2.13 — 'dehino 'smin yatha dehe kaumaram yauvanam jara, tatha dehantara-praptih...' Cited for the soul's transmigration through the bodies of a baby, boy, youth, and old man, and then into another body at death.
Bhagavad-gita 8.6 — 'yam yam vapi smaran bhavam tyajaty ante kalevaram...' Cited that whatever mentality/desire one holds at the moment of death determines one's next body.

Mahabharata — Yaksha Prashna (Vana Parva): the account of Yudhishthira answering the questions of Yamaraja/Dharmaraja; the most amazing thing in the world is that everyone sees others go to the kingdom of death yet each thinks he will live here forever.

Brihan-naradiya Purana — 'harer nama harer nama harer namaiva kevalam, kalau nasty eva nasty eva nasty eva gatir anyatha.' Cited (as ancient Purana) that in Kali-yuga chanting the holy name is the only means of deliverance.

Srimad Bhagavatam 12.3.51 — 'kaler dosha-nidhe rajann asti hy eko mahan gunah, kirtanad eva krishnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet.' Sukadeva Goswami tells Maharaja Parikshit that Kali is an ocean of faults but has one great quality: chanting Krishna's names grants liberation.

Srimad Bhagavatam 11.5.32 — 'krishna-varnam tvishakrishnam sangopangastra-parshadam, yajnaih sankirtana-prayair yajanti hi su-medhasah.' Cited as the verse foretelling the golden (recent) avatar, Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, worshiped through sankirtana.
Srimad Bhagavatam (named) — the setting of Maharaja Parikshit, cursed by a brahmana boy to die within seven days, hearing the Bhagavatam from Sukadeva Goswami at the Ganges.
Chaitanya-caritamrita, Madhya-lila 20.108 — 'jivera svarupa haya krishnera nitya-dasa.' Quoted that the living entity is by nature the eternal servant of Krishna.
Chaitanya-caritamrita (named) — cited as the culminating scripture describing the different rasas (mellows) of love of God.
Narottama Dasa Thakura's bhajan — 'golokera prema-dhana, hari-nama-sankirtana.' Quoted that the sankirtana movement is the treasure of the spiritual world Goloka, not a sectarian Indian invention.
Chanakya Pandit / niti-shastra — cited for the principle that one gives up something only when receiving something better, applied to renouncing bad habits through the higher taste of chanting.

Hare Krishna maha-mantra — 'Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.' Given as the means to attain the higher taste that sustains spiritual life.
